PHSCS 587

Diffusion and the Einstein relation

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a concentration gradient moves electrons even without an applied field

Random microscopic motion produces a net particle flow from higher to lower concentration. For electrons in one dimension, Fick’s law is Γn = −Dn dn/dx, where Γn is particle flux in m⁻²s⁻¹ and Dn is the diffusion coefficient in m²/s. Multiplying by electron charge gives conventional diffusion current Jn,diff = +qDn dn/dx. The arrows in the figure point in opposite directions because electron charge is negative.

For holes, Γp = −Dp dp/dx and Jp,diff = −qDp dp/dx. Including drift gives Jn = qμnnEfield + qDn dn/dx and Jp = qμppEfield − qDp dp/dx. These current densities are in A/m² when SI units are used throughout. A concentration gradient and a field can oppose each other, including the zero-current balance inside an equilibrium junction.

For nondegenerate carriers at uniform temperature in the low-field drift–diffusion model, Dn/μn = Dp/μp = kBT/q = VT. VT is the thermal voltage, about 25.9 mV at 300 K. The Einstein relation connects fluctuation-driven spreading to field-driven response. Degeneracy or hot carriers require a generalized relation.

Example

At 300 K, an illustrative mobility of 800 cm²/(V·s) corresponds to D ≈ 20.7 cm²/s through D = μVT. Keep the centimetre units in both μ and D, or convert both to SI.

Practice

1. If electron concentration decreases toward +x, which way do electron diffusion flux and current point?

Evaluate dn/dx, then include electron charge.

The gradient is negative, so Γn points toward +x and Jn,diff points toward −x.

2. Why do D/μ and kBT/q have compatible units?

Divide m²/s by m²/(V·s).

The mobility ratio has units V; energy divided by charge is also a volt.
